column4: The source section names ص ل و as the root that also carries fire; here صَلُّوهُ orders him into Hell, making the fire-sense audible in the name musallīn.
This repeats the section’s wording about not urging food for the miskīn; the refusal is named beside the punishment, while the source links miskīn’s root س ك ن to a fire people settle beside.
In Hell they say لَمْ نَكُ مِنَ الْمُصَلِّينَ; the source names musallīn and its fire-bearing root, while this confession gives the prayer failure behind the punishment.
They confess they did not feed the miskīn, echoing the source’s food and poor image; its root س ك ن also carries the section’s hearth association.
The verse turns wrongful consumption of orphan wealth into fire in the belly and a coming searing; the source’s ordinary food and hearth are reversed into punishment.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend face a warning of painful punishment; the source likewise moves from withheld household provision to fire.
Here hoarded wealth is heated in the Fire and used to brand its holders; 9:34 supplies the hoarding that this punishment answers.
The command أَلْقِيَا فِي جَهَنَّمَ places the condemned figure in Hell; 50:25 identifies him as a preventer of good, completing the source’s withholding-to-fire link.
The condemned person is called مَنَّاعٍ لِلْخَيْرِ, a preventer of good; 50:24 supplies the command to cast him into Hell, matching the withheld shared hearth and its consequence.
The section itself names بَخِلَ وَاسْتَغْنَىٰ as where this surah’s path begins; the tight-fisted self-sufficient person stands behind the withheld pot and ladle.
The warning names نَارًا تَلَظَّىٰ, a blazing fire; 92:15-16 identify who burns there and why.
The source’s ص ل و root appears in لَا يَصْلَاهَا, the act of entering and burning in that fire.
The one who burns is described as having denied and turned away; 92:14-15 supply the warning and fire, linking refusal to the source’s outcome.
The source names the cry وَيْل; here the same woe falls on deniers, the first step in a passage that then names their burning.
The source’s root ص ل و appears in لَصَالُوا الْجَحِيمِ, explicitly describing the condemned as burning in Hell.
After the burning, they are told this is what they used to deny; 83:16 contributes the fire, making denial meet its consequence.
The source names ص ل و as fire; سَأُصْلِيهِ سَقَرَ uses that root for making a person burn in Saqar.
Saqar is described as لَوَّاحَةٌ لِلْبَشَرِ, scorching human skin; 74:26 names the fire, giving bodily force to the source’s heat and roasting image.
When urged to give from their provision, the deniers refuse to feed those God could feed; that answer closely echoes the source’s withheld food before its turn to fire.
The wording وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ repeats the failure to urge feeding the poor, with the source’s miskīn root س ك ن adding the hearth association.
Here the righteous give food to the miskīn, orphan, and captive, the opposite of withholding the meal and shared hearth in the source.
The passage commends feeding in a day of hunger, reversing the source’s failure to urge food for the poor.
The source names al-muṣallīn; here the same word introduces those who pray as a commendable group, unlike the heedless prayer people of the source.
Their wealth has an acknowledged right; 70:25 assigns it to petitioners and deprived people, a direct counter-image to withholding the pot and ladle.
The next verse names the recipients as سَائِلٍ وَالْمَحْرُومِ, making the share in 70:24 concrete against the source’s unfed poor.
This warning names لَظَىٰ, the flame that 70:16 says strips skin, making the source’s change from hearth to harm bodily.
The flame strips away the skin; 70:15 names the fire, echoing the source’s fire-roasted meat and endured heat.
The fire’s fuel is people and stones rather than household fuel, reversing the source’s ordinary hearth and making the movement from useful fire to punishment explicit.
The command to protect one’s family from a fire fueled by people and stones turns the household hearth into its opposite.
They eat only fire into their bellies; this reverses the source’s cooked meal into punishment.
The source’s fire root ص ل و appears in تَصْلَىٰ نَارًا حَامِيَةً, a person burning in fierce heat.
Their only food is thorny plant; 88:4-5 place it in a burning, boiling setting, an opposite to the source’s nourishing shared meal.
The Zaqqum tree introduces a judgment meal; 44:44 calls it sinners’ food, reversing the source’s ordinary hearth and cooked meat.
The tree is explicitly طَعَامُ الْأَثِيمِ, food for the sinner; 44:43 introduces it and 44:45-46 make its heat bodily.
The sinner is dragged to the middle of Hell; 44:43-46 have already made the meal and its boiling explicit, joining food to the fire destination.
Boiling water is poured over his head after he is dragged to Hell; 44:47 supplies the destination and this verse completes the heat scene.
The deniers’ meal is from the Zaqqum tree, reversing the source’s hearth food into punishment; 56:54-56 make the boiling and judgment setting explicit.
This meal is named their hospitality on the Day of Judgment; 56:52-55 show the food and drink, contrasting with the home hearth’s hospitality.
The verse asks about the fire people kindle, directly meeting the source’s domestic fire and its ordinary uses.
The fire is made مَتَاعًا لِلْمُقْوِينَ, provision for travelers; 56:71-72 identify it as kindled and created, an explicit useful-fire counterpart to the punishment fire.
Their welcome is boiling water, a dreadful inversion of food and hospitality at the source’s hearth; 56:94 names Hellfire next.
The source’s root ص ل و appears in تَصْلِيَةُ جَحِيمٍ, explicitly naming burning in Hell after the boiling-water welcome of 56:93.
The question contrasts good hospitality with the Zaqqum tree; it brings the source’s hearth and meal image into a stark judgment reversal.
Their return is to Hell after the meal; 37:66-67 supply the food and boiling drink, completing the source’s food-to-fire reversal.
The source’s word وَيْل recurs over the wealth-hoarder of this passage; 104:2 and 104:4-6 connect the hoarding to kindled fire.
This person amasses and counts wealth, giving a concrete form of the source’s withholding before the fire scene in 104:4-9.
He is flung into al-Ḥuṭamah; 104:5-6 identify it as God’s kindled fire, turning the source’s woe into a fire scene.
The answer is نَارُ اللَّهِ الْمُوقَدَةُ, kindled fire; 104:4 names the person flung into it, echoing the source’s useful hearth turned punishment.
The source’s root ص ل و appears in سَيَصْلَىٰ نَارًا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ, a direct statement that he will burn in a flaming fire.
The source dictionary form الصلاء includes fuel; this verse calls her حَمَّالَةَ الْحَطَبِ, a carrier of firewood in the same punishment scene.
The source’s root ص ل و appears in صِلِيًّا for burning; the verse identifies who is most deserving of that fire.
The source’s root ص ل و appears in اصْلَوْهَا; the command says to burn there whether patient or impatient, directly meeting its dictionary sense of bearing heat.
The source’s fire root ص ل و appears in يَصْلَوْنَهَا, burning on the Day of Judgment.
The source’s root ص ل و appears in وَيَصْلَىٰ سَعِيرًا, the burning fate of the person given the record from behind.
He thought he would never return to God; 84:12 names the fire he faces, linking denial of return to the source’s judgment and fire image.
The source’s root ص ل و appears in يَصْلَى النَّارَ الْكُبْرَىٰ, burning in the greatest fire.
The fire repeatedly cooks the skin until it is replaced so the person can taste punishment; the source’s cooking and roasting branch turns from meat to the one facing fire.
God commands Abraham’s fire to be coolness and safety; this is a specific reversal of the source’s ordinary heat and its final burning punishment.
Moses sees a fire and hopes to bring a brand so his family may تَصْطَلُونَ, matching the source dictionary form اصطليت بالنار for warming at a hearth.
Moses promises a firebrand لَعَلَّكُمْ تَصْطَلُونَ, the same warming scene and root sense as the source’s اصطليت بالنار.
This commands seizure and binding before 69:31’s burning; the row supplies the approach to the image’s final fire.
The chain follows the command to burn him; 69:31 contributes the Hellfire, and this verse continues the punishment beyond entry.
The fire sequence names disbelief in God as a reason; 69:34 adds failure to urge food for the poor, placing this cause beside the shared-hearth image.
These are those who deny the Day of Judgment, echoing the larger surah’s opening denier; 83:16-17 complete this passage’s path to fire.
After the tight-fisted person of 92:8 comes denial of the best; it develops the path toward the fire warned of in 92:14.
This says the tight-fisted denier is eased toward hardship; the following fire passage makes that hard end concrete.
His wealth will not avail when he falls; it sharpens the source’s claim that one who withholds provision ultimately faces fire.
Saqar leaves nothing and spares nothing; 74:26 names the fire and 74:29 its scorching effect, extending the punishment scene around the source’s final fire.
They confess that they denied the Day of Recompense; 74:43-44 place failure to pray and feed the poor in the same account of those facing punishment.
They explain that they feed others only for God’s sake; 76:8 gives the act, contrasting selfless sharing with the source’s household refusal.
The next verse identifies an orphan near of kin as one who receives that food, specifying the vulnerable neighbor absent from the withheld hearth.
The sequence names a miskīn in the dust as another recipient; the source’s miskīn root س ك ن is heard here against refusal to share food.
These prayerful people are constant in their prayer; 70:22 introduces the group whose care for others contrasts with the source’s prayer name over a fire image.
The next verse calls this a trade of guidance for error and punishment; 2:174 supplies the image of fire eaten as food.
The fire-bound person is given water from a boiling spring; 88:4 supplies the burning and 88:6-7 the failed meal, reversing the household food scene.
This food neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger; 88:6 identifies it, contrasting the source’s meal withheld from the poor.
This food boils in the belly like molten metal; 44:44 names it as a meal, turning the source’s cooking image into punishment.
The meal boils like حمِيم; 44:45 gives the belly where it boils, extending the source’s fire and food image.
The command ذُقْ tells him to taste the punishment; 44:48 supplies the boiling water, echoing the source’s tasting and enduring fire senses.
The punishment is identified as what they doubted; 44:49 commands them to taste it, joining denial to the source’s fire consequence.
They fill their bellies from this food; 56:52 names the meal, turning the source’s cooking and sharing image inward.
They drink boiling water over the meal; 56:52-53 supply the food and full bellies, continuing the inverted feast.
They drink like thirsty camels; 56:54 supplies the boiling drink, extending the punishment meal linked against the source’s hearth.
It asks who created the fire’s tree; 56:71 names the kindled fire and 56:73 gives its provision for travelers.
The condemned group is called deniers gone astray; 56:93-94 give their fiery reception, joining denial to the source’s end.
The sinners eat from the tree and fill their bellies; 37:62 introduces the rival meal and 37:67-68 complete the Hell setting.
Their meal is mixed with boiling water; 37:66 gives the eating, transforming the source’s cooked food into torment.
He thinks wealth will make him last forever; 104:2 names the accumulation and 104:4-9 overturn that confidence with fire.
The question asks what al-Ḥuṭamah is; 104:6 answers with kindled fire, defining the punishment that follows the source’s withholding image.
The fire rises over hearts; 104:6 names its kindling, extending the endured-heat image of the source.
The fire is closed over them; 104:6-7 supply the fire and its reach, continuing the punishment scene.
They are confined among extended pillars; 104:8 supplies the closure around the fire, completing this sustained punishment scene.
His wealth will not avail him; 111:3-4 bring the fire and its fuel, paralleling the source’s refusal to share provision before facing fire.
The condemned are not absent from that fire; 82:15 names the burning, extending its inescapable heat.
This person receives his record from behind; 84:12 gives the fire that follows, resembling the source’s cited record-to-Hell sequence in Hāqqah.
He cries out for destruction before the fire named in 84:12, continuing the record-to-punishment sequence.
He had been joyful among his people; 84:14 says he thought he would not return, explaining the stance beside 84:12’s fire fate.
In that fire he neither dies nor lives; 87:12 names the burning, giving a stark form to the source’s bearing of heat and severity.
Moses asks his family to wait while he seeks a firebrand; warmth is not stated here, but the household fire carried back is a plausible parallel to the source’s hearth image.
The verse heats iron with bellows and pours molten copper to form a barrier; it does not straighten a stick, but it is a specific parallel to the source’s fire softening material so it can be shaped.
